paras: The reported Hinesville lynching of 1888 was an account, carried by Georgia and Midwestern papers in February 1888, that armed men had seized a Black man accused of arson from a deputy sheriff in Liberty County, Georgia, and killed him. In November 1888 the Savannah Morning News reported that the lynching story had proved untrue and that the accused, George Washington, had been convicted of arson and sentenced to life.

Late in January 1888 a fire at Johnston's Station, on the Savannah, Florida and Western railway, destroyed James Chapman's store, the railway company's warehouse and several other buildings. The fire was suspected to be the work of an incendiary, and the Atlanta Constitution reported that "The people have been greatly wrought up in consequence."

A Black man was arrested on suspicion on Wednesday, according to a Savannah dispatch dated February 10, or on Tuesday, according to the Atlanta Constitution. Both accounts said he confessed at a preliminary hearing, and the Constitution added that he implicated several others. While a deputy sheriff had him in charge, on the way to the Hinesville jail in one version and after his commitment to it in the other, a group of men took him away; the Savannah dispatch counted "a crowd of fifteen men," the Constitution "a band of armed men."

The men carried the prisoner into the woods. The Savannah dispatch did not report a body and said only that "it is supposed that he was hanged or burned," while the Constitution stated that the men "shot him to death." A wire digest put the seizure "on the 8th" and said he was taken from jail and "riddled with bullets."

No report of an inquest or of arrests of the men who took the prisoner appears in the coverage. When the Liberty County superior court adjourned in November 1888, the Savannah Morning News reported that George Washington, William Fields and Julius McLary had been convicted of arson and sentenced to the penitentiary for life. The paper identified Washington as the man who had burned the warehouse and Chapman's store and wrote that he "was reported to have been lynched," but "the report proved untrue, and he was afterward run down by the officers." It described Fields and McLary as his accomplices and said Washington had escaped after the fire, without explaining how he had come out of the February seizure.

The story reached Northern readers first through the Savannah dispatch, which the Waterbury Evening Democrat ran on February 10 under the headline "An Incendiar's Fate." The Atlanta Constitution included it in its "Dixie Doings" column of Georgia news on February 14, stressing the local excitement and stating the killing as fact. A one-sentence version then circulated in weekly news digests, appearing word for word in the Mower County Transcript, the Kanabec County Times, the Big Stone City Herald and the Griggs Courier between February 15 and 17.

None of these reports named the prisoner, and each identified him only as "a negro." The correction came nine months later in a single sentence of a Savannah court roundup headlined for a different case, and no correction appears in the papers that had carried the digest item.

The February accounts disagree on how the prisoner died, giving hanging or burning as a supposition in the Savannah dispatch and shooting in the Constitution and the digest. The Savannah Morning News report of November, a later local account tied to a court verdict, holds that he was not lynched at all.

bases: February reports described an armed band seizing an arson suspect from a deputy sheriff and killing him (A1, A2, A3), but a later Savannah court report says the lynching report proved untrue and the man was later captured and convicted (A7), so this is at most a seizure or attempted lynching that was reported as a completed one.

February reports said a band of armed men, fifteen in one account, took an accused incendiary from a deputy and killed or were supposed to have killed him (A1, A2, A3), but the Savannah Morning News, reporting his arson conviction in November, said 'The report proved untrue' (A7); the later local court report outweighs the early dispatches, one of which never claimed a body was found (A1).

Two independent February reports agree that armed men took the prisoner from a deputy (A1, A2) and a wire digest says he was shot (A3), but a later local report states that the lynching report was untrue and that the man was convicted of arson (A7).

framing.detail: The Savannah dispatch ran under the headline 'An Incendiar's Fate', treating the man's confession as settled and his death as a supposition.
The Atlanta Constitution placed the item in a regional column, stressing local excitement over the fire and stating the killing as fact.
Minnesota and Dakota weeklies ran an identical one-sentence digest item, 'riddled with bullets', among unrelated news of the week.
The Savannah Morning News corrected the lynching report in one sentence of a routine court roundup headlined for a different case.
